summary: Describes how to build PPP sessions and encapsulate PPP packets over Ethernet. It is widely used by broadband providers to connect customers over shared Ethernet-style links. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Dial-up style logins used to work over phone lines. This document shows how to do the same sign-in and conversation over an Ethernet cable instead.

subtitle: How to run PPP sessions over Ethernet, with a discovery handshake to find the other end.

tldr.problem: Broadband access providers want dial-up style per-user sessions, with access control and billing, over a shared Ethernet that connects several hosts through a simple bridging device.
tldr.mechanism: PPPoE first runs a four-step Discovery stage to learn the access concentrator's Ethernet address and a session ID. PPP frames are then carried inside Ethernet frames tagged with that session ID.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is Informational and describes the encapsulation being deployed by RedBack Networks, RouterWare, UUNET and others at the time. It is not an Internet standard.

today: RFC 2516 is an Informational RFC, not an Internet standard. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. When it was written, the text says the encapsulation was being deployed by RedBack Networks, RouterWare, UUNET and others.

sections.title: Why PPP Over Ethernet
sections.content:
Access technologies have conflicting goals. Several hosts at a site should share one customer premise access device, access control and billing should work like dial-up PPP, and the device should be cheap and need little or no configuration. Ethernet is the most cost effective way to attach the hosts.

PPP over Ethernet (PPPoE) lets a network of hosts connect over a simple bridging device to a remote Access Concentrator. Each host runs its own PPP stack, so the user sees a familiar interface, and access control, billing and type of service can be done per user rather than per site.

PPP assumes a point-to-point link, while Ethernet is multi-access. So each session must learn the Ethernet address of its remote peer and establish a unique session identifier, which is what PPPoE's discovery protocol provides.
sections.plainLanguage: A shared cable lets many computers talk, but the provider wants a private chat with each person. PPPoE sets up that private chat on top of the shared cable.

sections.title: Two Stages
sections.content:
PPPoE has a Discovery stage and a PPP Session stage. In Discovery the Host (the client) finds an Access Concentrator (the server), learns its Ethernet MAC address and establishes a SESSION_ID. Several Access Concentrators may answer, so the Host can discover all of them and pick one.

Discovery stays stateless until a PPP session is established. At that point both the Host and the Access Concentrator MUST allocate resources for a PPP virtual interface.
sections.plainLanguage: Step one is finding out who you are talking to and getting a ticket number. Step two is the real conversation using that ticket number.

sections.title: Frames and the PPPoE Header
sections.content:
Discovery frames use Ethernet type 0x8863 and session frames use 0x8864. The Ethernet destination is either unicast or the broadcast address, and for session traffic it MUST be the peer's unicast address learned in Discovery.

The PPPoE payload starts with a 4-bit VER and a 4-bit TYPE, both MUST be 0x1. Next come an 8-bit CODE, a 16-bit SESSION_ID and a 16-bit LENGTH. The session ID is fixed for a session and, with the two Ethernet addresses, defines it. The value 0xffff is reserved and MUST NOT be used. LENGTH counts only the PPPoE payload, not the Ethernet or PPPoE headers.

Discovery payloads hold zero or more TAGs, each a type-length-value item with a 16-bit type and a 16-bit length. A TAG of unknown type MUST be ignored, which keeps new tags backwards compatible.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message has a small label saying what kind it is, which session it belongs to and how long it is. Discovery messages can also carry extra labelled notes called tags.

sections.title: The Discovery Handshake
sections.content:
Discovery has four steps. The Host broadcasts a PADI (Initiation) packet, with code 0x09 and session ID zero. It must contain exactly one Service-Name TAG and MUST NOT exceed 1484 octets, leaving room for a relay agent to add a Relay-Session-Id TAG.

Each Access Concentrator that can serve it replies with a unicast PADO (Offer), code 0x07, containing an AC-Name TAG and the Service-Name. One that cannot serve the request MUST NOT answer. The Host picks one, based on the AC-Name or the services offered, and sends a PADR (Request), code 0x19, to it.

The Access Concentrator generates a unique session ID and replies with a PADS (Session-confirmation), code 0x65. If it dislikes the Service-Name it replies with a Service-Name-Error TAG and session ID zero. Either side may later send a PADT (Terminate), code 0xa7, naming the session. After a PADT no more PPP traffic may be sent on that session, not even normal PPP termination packets.
sections.plainLanguage: The computer shouts, who can connect me? Any provider box that can help answers. The computer picks one and asks it for a session number, and the box hands one out.

sections.title: Session Stage, LCP and Timeouts
sections.content:
Once the session begins, PPP data is sent as in any other PPP encapsulation. All Ethernet frames are unicast, the Ethernet type is 0x8864, the PPPoE code MUST be 0x00, and the session ID MUST NOT change. The PPPoE payload is a PPP frame that begins with the PPP Protocol-ID.

The Magic Number LCP option is RECOMMENDED and Protocol Field Compression is NOT RECOMMENDED. Implementations MUST NOT request, and MUST reject, FCS Alternatives, Address-and-Control-Field-Compression and Asynchronous-Control-Character-Map. The PPP MTU MUST NOT exceed 1492, since Ethernet's maximum payload is 1500 octets minus the 6-octet PPPoE header and the 2-octet PPP Protocol ID. The Access Concentrator is RECOMMENDED to send occasional Echo-Requests, because a Host that quits without a Terminate-Request would otherwise go unnoticed.

When LCP ends, both sides MUST stop using the session, and a Host wanting a new one MUST return to Discovery. If no PADO arrives in time, the Host SHOULD resend its PADI and double the waiting period. A similar timeout applies while waiting for a PADS, after which the Host SHOULD fall back to resending a PADI.
sections.plainLanguage: After the setup, normal chat flows inside the session. The message size is a little smaller than usual because the PPPoE label takes some room. If the chat ends, you must start from the beginning to chat again.

sections.title: Denial of Service and Service Names
sections.content:
To resist denial-of-service attacks, the Access Concentrator can use the AC-Cookie TAG. It SHOULD be able to regenerate the value from the PADR source address, so it can check the sender is reachable and then limit concurrent sessions for that address. The algorithm is left to the implementation. One example is HMAC over the Host MAC address with a secret key. The RFC states that the cookie cannot stop every such attack, so other protective means MAY be used.

Many Access Concentrators will not want to reveal their services to an unauthenticated party. They should either never refuse a request because of its Service-Name TAG and always echo the value sent (the RECOMMENDED policy), or accept only requests with a zero-length Service-Name, meaning any service.
sections.plainLanguage: The provider box gives each caller a secret stamp it can check later, so a fake caller cannot flood it with requests. It also avoids revealing which services it offers to strangers.
